```{r}
#| output: false
#| echo: false

library(renv)
renv::load()
library(targets)
library(here)
tar_config_set(
  store = here::here("_targets")
)
source(here::here("R", "analyse-coux.R"))
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(forcats)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggrepel)
library(bipartite)

guild_colors <- c(pollinator = "#2a78d6", plant = "#eb6834")
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 11))
```

The data contains 5 different tables, that we can group in three categories:

1. plant-pollinator interaction list at each site
2. plant and pollinator abundances (one table per guild)
3. plant and pollinator traits (one table per guild)

We look at each of these categories in what follows.

```{r}
data <- tar_read(data_coux)
head(data$interaction)
```

## Abundances

We have plant presence/absence per site — despite the name, this is
binary (1/0), not a count.

```{r}
str(data$plant_abundance)
```

And pollinator abundances, which are actual counts.

```{r}
str(data$pollinator_abundance)
```

### Plant occurence

```{r}
n_sites_abundance <- n_distinct(data$plant_abundance$site)

plant_occupancy <- data$plant_abundance |>
  pivot_longer(-site, names_to = "plant", values_to = "present") |>
  group_by(plant) |>
  summarise(n_sites = sum(present), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(plant = fct_reorder(plant, n_sites))

ggplot(plant_occupancy, aes(x = plant, y = n_sites)) +
  geom_col(fill = guild_colors[["plant"]], width = 0.7) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    x = NULL, y = paste0("Number of sites (out of ", n_sites_abundance, ")")
  )
```

Most plant species are recorded at the majority of sites, unlike
pollinators below, where a few generalists dominate and many species are
site-specific.

### Pollinator abundance

```{r}
pollinator_totals <- data$pollinator_abundance |>
  pivot_longer(-site, names_to = "pollinator", values_to = "abundance") |>
  group_by(pollinator) |>
  summarise(total_abundance = sum(abundance), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(pollinator = fct_reorder(pollinator, total_abundance))

ggplot(pollinator_totals, aes(x = pollinator, y = total_abundance)) +
  geom_col(fill = guild_colors[["pollinator"]], width = 0.7) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(trans = "log1p", breaks = c(0, 10, 100, 1000, 10000)) +
  labs(
    x = NULL, y = "Total abundance across sites (log scale)"
  )
```

## Interactions

Here is what the raw data looks like.


```{r}
#| echo: false
n_sites <- n_distinct(data$interaction$site)
n_pollinators <- n_distinct(data$interaction$pollinator)
n_plants <- n_distinct(data$interaction$plant)
prop_zero <- mean(data$interaction$links == 0)
```

The columns correspond to

- `site`: the community (`r n_sites` sites)
- `pollinator`: the pollinator species (`r n_pollinators` species across all sites)
- `plant`: the plant species (`r n_plants` species across all sites)
- `links`: the number of interaction events (visits) observed between that
  plant and that pollinator at that site (`r scales::percent(prop_zero)` show
zero observed visits).

::: {.callout-note}

`data_coux` is already cleaned by `clean_coux_data()`: species names are
lowercased everywhere (pollinator names are capitalised and plant names
inconsistently so in the raw data), and `alnus_glutinosa`/`alnus_serrulate` are
merged into a single `alnus_sp`. The raw interaction table has `alnus_glutinosa`
at site `blahamlak` with no matching trait/abundance row, and `alnus_serrulate`
at `crobirlee`/`crostelee` joining fine. Since no site uses both names, we treat
all three as the same plant recorded under two names. See `clean_coux_data()` in
`R/analyse-coux.R` for details; use `tar_read(data_coux_raw)` to see the
uncleaned version.

:::

We have coded a function to compute species level network metrics using the
`bipartite::specieslevel` function.

```{r}
net_metrics <- tar_read(net_metrics)
net_metrics
```

### Site richness

```{r}
site_richness <- data$interaction |>
  group_by(site) |>
  summarise(
    pollinator = n_distinct(pollinator),
    plant = n_distinct(plant),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(pollinator, plant),
    names_to = "guild",
    values_to = "n_species"
  ) |>
  mutate(site = fct_reorder(site, n_species, .fun = sum))

ggplot(site_richness, aes(x = site, y = n_species, fill = guild)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", width = 0.7) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = guild_colors) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Number of species", fill = NULL) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), legend.position = "top")
```

Sites range from a few species to much richer communities. Network size itself
is a potential confound to keep in mind in later analyses. We also note that
plant and pollinator richness are strongly positively correlated.

### Interaction matrices

```{r}
ggplot(data$interaction, aes(x = links)) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 1, fill = guild_colors[["pollinator"]],
    color = "white", linewidth = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(trans = "sqrt") +
  labs(
    x = "Observed visits (links)", y = "Number of pairs (sqrt scale)"
  )
```

### Degree distribution by guild

```{r}
ggplot(net_metrics, aes(x = guild, y = degree, fill = guild)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = guild_colors) +
  labs(
    x = NULL, y = "Degree (number of partners)"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

### Degree per species

As for uniqueness and originality above, each species has one degree value
per site it occurs at, so we look at the per-species distribution across
sites, ordered by median within each guild.

```{r}
degree_by_species <- net_metrics |>
  mutate(species = fct_reorder(species, degree, .fun = median))

ggplot(degree_by_species, aes(x = species, y = degree, fill = guild)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = guild_colors) +
  facet_wrap(~guild, scales = "free_y") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Degree (number of partners)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

### Normalised degree per species

Raw degree is mechanically capped by how many species a site has at all, so
we also look at normalised degree — degree scaled by the number of possible
partners at that site — which partially controls for that site-richness
confound.

```{r}
ndegree_by_species <- net_metrics |>
  mutate(species = fct_reorder(species, normalised_degree, .fun = median))

ggplot(ndegree_by_species, aes(x = species, y = normalised_degree, fill = guild)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = guild_colors) +
  facet_wrap(~guild, scales = "free_y") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Normalised degree") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

### Specialisation (d′) per species

Same, for Blüthgen's d′. d′ is `NA` for species in the three smallest
networks (all of a species' partners are only ever visited by it, leaving
the normalisation undefined), which `median()`/the boxplot silently drop.

```{r}
dprime_by_species <- net_metrics |>
  mutate(species = fct_reorder(species, d_prime, .fun = median, na.rm = TRUE))

ggplot(dprime_by_species, aes(x = species, y = d_prime, fill = guild)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = guild_colors) +
  facet_wrap(~guild, scales = "free_y") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Specialisation (Blüthgen's d′)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

### Specificity (HS) per species

HS is the Shannon-based specificity used by @Coux-etal-2016, from Poisot's
`ESM` package:

$$ \text{HS}_i = 1 - \frac{H_i}{\log R} $$

where $H_i$ is the Shannon entropy of species $i$'s visits across plants and
$R$ is the number of plants visited by anyone at the site. A species with a
single partner has HS = 1 (a perfect specialist); one spreading its visits
evenly over every available plant has HS = 0. Unlike d′, it does not
correct for how often each partner is visited overall. See `compute_hs()`.

```{r}
hs_by_species <- net_metrics |>
  mutate(species = fct_reorder(species, hs, .fun = median))

ggplot(hs_by_species, aes(x = species, y = hs, fill = guild)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = guild_colors) +
  facet_wrap(~guild, scales = "free_y") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Specificity (HS)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

### An example network

The richest site, for a sense of what an actual interaction web looks like.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6.5

web_list <- tar_read(web_list)
richest_site <- names(web_list)[which.max(vapply(web_list, sum, numeric(1)))]

plotweb(
  web_list[[richest_site]],
  higher_color = guild_colors[["pollinator"]],
  lower_color = guild_colors[["plant"]],
  link_color = "grey80",
  srt = 0,
  text_size = 1
)
```


## Trait overview

We have plant traits: growth form, phenology, flower morphology and
nectar reward (14 plants).

```{r}
str(data$plant_trait)
```

We have pollinator traits: body size, foraging preferences, sociality
and larval diet (16 pollinators).

```{r}
str(data$pollinator_trait)
```

### Plant types and annual vs perennial

```{r}
ggplot(
  data$plant_trait,
  aes(x = fct_infreq(growth_form), fill = annual_perennial)
) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(
    x = NULL, y = "Number of species", fill = NULL
  )
```

### Most pollinators are small-bodied and solitary

```{r}
ggplot(data$pollinator_trait, aes(x = body_length, fill = soc_sol)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  labs(
    x = "Body length (mm)", y = "Number of species", fill = NULL
  )
```

## Trait spaces

We follow Coux et al. (2016)'s approach: traits are standardised and combined
into a single dissimilarity via Gower's distance, then ordinated with PCoA. To
see how each trait contributes to the two ordination axes, we fit every trait
separately onto the PCoA scores

### Plant trait space

```{r}
plant_trait_ready <- tar_read(plant_trait_ready)
plant_pcoa <- tar_read(plant_trait_pcoa)
plant_pct <- round(plant_pcoa$values$Rel_corr_eig[1:2] * 100, 1)

plant_pcoa_df <- as.data.frame(plant_pcoa$vectors[, 1:2])
names(plant_pcoa_df) <- c("Axis1", "Axis2")
plant_pcoa_df$plant <- rownames(plant_pcoa_df)
plant_pcoa_df$growth_form <- plant_trait_ready$growth_form

ggplot(plant_pcoa_df, aes(Axis1, Axis2, color = growth_form, label = plant)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_text_repel(size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = paste0("PCoA1 (", plant_pct[1], "%)"),
    y = paste0("PCoA2 (", plant_pct[2], "%)"),
    color = NULL
  )
```

Trees cluster tightly together, while herbs are more spread out — reflecting
probably a more variable growth strategy within that group.

### Which traits drive the plant trait space

```{r}
plant_fit <- tar_read(plant_trait_fit)
plot_trait_importance(plant_fit)
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6.5

plot_trait_biplot(plant_pcoa, plant_fit, guild_colors[["plant"]])
```

Season splits the space along a diagonal (spring/winter-flowering species
vs. the rest), while growth form and inflorescence type separate species
mostly along PCoA1 — consistent with the tree/herb split seen above.

### Pollinator trait space

```{r}
pollinator_trait_ready <- tar_read(pollinator_trait_ready)
pollinator_pcoa <- tar_read(pollinator_trait_pcoa)
pollinator_pct <- round(pollinator_pcoa$values$Rel_corr_eig[1:2] * 100, 1)

pollinator_pcoa_df <- as.data.frame(pollinator_pcoa$vectors[, 1:2])
names(pollinator_pcoa_df) <- c("Axis1", "Axis2")
pollinator_pcoa_df$pollinator <- rownames(pollinator_pcoa_df)
pollinator_pcoa_df$soc_sol <- pollinator_trait_ready$soc_sol

ggplot(
  pollinator_pcoa_df,
  aes(Axis1, Axis2, color = soc_sol, label = pollinator)
) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_text_repel(size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = paste0("PCoA1 (", pollinator_pct[1], "%)"),
    y = paste0("PCoA2 (", pollinator_pct[2], "%)"),
    color = NULL
  )
```

### Which traits drive the pollinator trait space

```{r}
pollinator_fit <- tar_read(pollinator_trait_fit)
plot_trait_importance(pollinator_fit)
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6.5

plot_trait_biplot(pollinator_pcoa, pollinator_fit, guild_colors[["pollinator"]])
```

## Uniqueness and originality

### Uniqueness

We compute species uniqueness per species per site. Uniqueness is defined as

$$ \text{uniqueness}_i = \min_j d_{ij} $$

that is the minimal functional distance to another species present in the
community. Following @Coux-etal-2016, $d_{ij}$ is the Euclidean distance in the
Cailliez-corrected PCoA space, the same space in which we compute originality
below, so that both metrics describe positions in a single trait space. A
species alone at its site has no neighbour and is left out.

```{r}
plant_uniqueness <- tar_read(plant_uniqueness)
pollinator_uniqueness <- tar_read(pollinator_uniqueness)
all_uniqueness <- rbind(
  plant_uniqueness |> mutate(guild = "plant"),
  pollinator_uniqueness |> mutate(guild = "pollinator")
) |>
  mutate(species = fct_reorder(species, uniqueness, .fun = median))

ggplot(all_uniqueness, aes(x = species, y = uniqueness, fill = guild)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = guild_colors) +
  facet_wrap(~guild, scales = "free_y") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Functional uniqueness") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

### Originality

Functional originality is the distance of a species from the trait centroid
of the community it belongs to, i.e. how much its traits differ from the
community's average:

$$ \text{originality}_i = \lVert x_i - \bar{x}_{\text{community}} \rVert $$

We compute it per species per site in the PCoA trait space, with the centroid
taken over the species present at each site.

```{r}
plant_originality <- tar_read(plant_originality)
pollinator_originality <- tar_read(pollinator_originality)
all_originality <- rbind(
  plant_originality |> mutate(guild = "plant"),
  pollinator_originality |> mutate(guild = "pollinator")
) |>
  mutate(species = fct_reorder(species, originality, .fun = median))

ggplot(all_originality, aes(x = species, y = originality, fill = guild)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = guild_colors) +
  facet_wrap(~guild, scales = "free_y") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Functional originality") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

### Weighted originality

Above, the community centroid treats every present species equally. For
pollinators we also have abundance data, so we can instead weight the
centroid by how common each species is at a site.

```{r}
pollinator_originality_w <- tar_read(pollinator_originality_w)

originality_comparison <- rbind(
  pollinator_originality |> mutate(weighting = "unweighted"),
  pollinator_originality_w |> mutate(weighting = "weighted by abundance")
) |>
  mutate(
    weighting = factor(
      weighting,
      levels = c("unweighted", "weighted by abundance")
    ),
    species_within = reorder(
      paste(species, weighting, sep = "___"), originality,
      FUN = median
    )
  )

ggplot(
  originality_comparison,
  aes(x = species_within, y = originality, fill = weighting)
) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "unweighted" = "grey60",
      "weighted by abundance" = guild_colors[["pollinator"]]
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = \(x) sub("___.*$", "", x)) +
  facet_wrap(~weighting, scales = "free_y") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Functional originality") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

We see that ranking shift with weighting. Common generalist, such `a_mellifera`
drop in originality as they pull the community weighted mean, while rarer
species such as `n_producta` increase in originality.

To check, to what extent species abundance drive their originality we plot
species weighted originality against their abundance for each site.

```{r}
pollinator_abundance <- data$pollinator_abundance |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = a_mellifera:t_orthodoxus,
    names_to = "species",
    values_to = "abundance"
  ) |>
  filter_out(abundance == 0)

originality_abundance <- pollinator_originality_w |>
  left_join(pollinator_abundance, by = join_by(site, species))

ggplot(
  originality_abundance,
  aes(x = log10(abundance), y = originality, color = species),
) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Abundance (log10 scale)",
    y = "Weighted originality",
    color = "Species"
  )
```

We see that there is strong negative correlation between weighted originality
and species abundance. This means that we should be careful if we use this
metric.

### Originality vs uniqueness

Next, we want to check that species originality and uniqueness are not too
strongly correlated, to ensure that the two metrics are complementary
description of species position in the functional space.

```{r}
pol_originality_uniqueness <- pollinator_originality |>
  left_join(pollinator_uniqueness, by = join_by(site, species))

plant_originality_uniqueness <- plant_originality |>
  left_join(plant_uniqueness, by = join_by(site, species))

originality_uniqueness <- rbind(
  plant_originality_uniqueness |> mutate(guild = "plant"),
  pol_originality_uniqueness |> mutate(guild = "pollinator")
)

ggplot(
  originality_uniqueness,
  aes(x = uniqueness, y = originality, color = guild)
) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Uniqueness", y = "Originality", color = "Guild")
```


```{r}
head(tar_read(net_metrics))
```

## Interaction niche

Following Dehling & Stouffer (2018) and Dehling et al. (2022), a species'
interaction niche describes it through the traits of its interaction
partners rather than its own traits: its *position* is the (link-weighted)
centroid of its partners' traits in the partner guild's trait space, its
*size* is how dispersed those partners are around that centroid, and its
*originality* is how far that centroid sits from the average position of
its guild-mates at the same site.

We use dispersion rather than a hull/hypervolume for niche size: partner
counts here are low (median degree 1-2.5 per the degree distributions
above), too low for a hull-based volume to be defined for most species,
whereas a dispersion-based measure degrades gracefully — a species with a
single partner simply gets a niche size of 0.

### Niche size

```{r}
plant_interaction_niche <- tar_read(plant_interaction_niche)
pollinator_interaction_niche <- tar_read(pollinator_interaction_niche)
all_interaction_niche <- rbind(
  plant_interaction_niche |> mutate(guild = "plant"),
  pollinator_interaction_niche |> mutate(guild = "pollinator")
)

niche_size_by_species <- all_interaction_niche |>
  mutate(species = fct_reorder(species, niche_size, .fun = median))

ggplot(niche_size_by_species, aes(x = species, y = niche_size, fill = guild)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = guild_colors) +
  facet_wrap(~guild, scales = "free_y") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Interaction niche size") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

### Niche originality

```{r}
niche_originality_by_species <- all_interaction_niche |>
  mutate(species = fct_reorder(species, niche_originality, .fun = median))

ggplot(
  niche_originality_by_species,
  aes(x = species, y = niche_originality, fill = guild)
) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = guild_colors) +
  facet_wrap(~guild, scales = "free_y") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Interaction niche originality") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

## Pollinator origin

We get for each species whether they are native to New-Zealand or have been
introduced. We do so to get a rough sense whether species native status might
drive some of the patterns we observe. This is motivated by the dominance of the
honeybee (A. Mellifera) which is an introduced species.

```{r}
pollinator_annotation <- tar_read(pollinator_annotation)
pollinator_annotation |>
  select(species_name, origin, origin_confidence) |>
  arrange(origin, species_name) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Eleven of the 16 pollinator species are introduced. They also make up more
than half of the pollinator species at 13 of the 21 sites.

```{r}
origin_share <- data$pollinator_abundance |>
  pivot_longer(-site, names_to = "pollinator", values_to = "abundance") |>
  filter(abundance > 0) |>
  mutate(presence = 1) |>
  left_join(pollinator_annotation, by = join_by(pollinator)) |>
  mutate(
    class = case_when(
      pollinator == "a_mellifera" ~ "A. mellifera",
      origin == "native" ~ "Native",
      origin == "introduced" ~ "Introduced"
    ),
    class = factor(class, levels = c("Native", "Introduced", "A. mellifera"))
  ) |>
  group_by(site, class) |>
  summarise(class_richness = sum(presence), .groups = "drop_last") |>
  mutate(share = class_richness / sum(class_richness)) |>
  ungroup()

native_order <- origin_share |>
  filter(class == "Native") |>
  arrange(share) |>
  pull(site)

origin_colors <- c(
  Native = "#3a9e5f", Introduced = "grey60", `A. mellifera` = "#d4a017"
)

site_order <- union(native_order, unique(origin_share$site))

p_share <- origin_share |>
  mutate(site = factor(site, levels = site_order)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = site, y = share, fill = class)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = origin_colors) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Share of pollinator species", fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

pollinator_richness <- site_richness |>
  filter(guild == "pollinator") |>
  mutate(site = factor(site, levels = site_order))

p_richness <- ggplot(pollinator_richness, aes(x = site, y = n_species)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7, fill = guild_colors[["pollinator"]]) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Pollinator richness") +
  theme(
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()
  )

cowplot::plot_grid(
  p_share, p_richness,
  nrow = 1, rel_widths = c(3, 1), align = "h", axis = "tb"
)
```

## Does functional originality predicts pollinator specialism

@Coux-etal-2016 report that a pollinator's functional originality predicts
its role in the network: its normalised degree (ND) and its specificity (HS).
Their models regress ND and HS on *abundance-weighted* originality and on
abundance, plus a few other terms with small effects that we leave aside
here.

```{r}
pollinator_trait_network <- tar_read(pollinator_trait_network)
trait_network_models <- tar_read(trait_network_models)
trait_network_models_richness <- tar_read(trait_network_models_richness)

# Format a coefficient as "mean [lower, upper]".
coef_text <- function(tbl, response, model, term) {
  row <- tbl[tbl$response == response & tbl$model == model &
    tbl$term == term, ]
  sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", row$mean, row$lower, row$upper)
}
spearman <- function(x, y) {
  sprintf("%.2f", cor(x, y, method = "spearman"))
}
```

### Weighted and unweighted originality

When weighting the community centroid by abundance an abundant species drags the
centroid towards itself. The more abundant you are, the closer you sit to the
centroid, and the less "original" you look.

```{r}
originality_vs_abundance <- pollinator_trait_network |>
  select(site, species, abundance, originality, originality_w) |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(originality, originality_w),
    names_to = "measure", values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    measure = factor(
      measure,
      levels = c("originality", "originality_w"),
      labels = c(
        paste0(
          "Unweighted (ρ = ",
          spearman(
            pollinator_trait_network$originality,
            log(pollinator_trait_network$abundance)
          ), ")"
        ),
        paste0(
          "Weighted by abundance (ρ = ",
          spearman(
            pollinator_trait_network$originality_w,
            log(pollinator_trait_network$abundance)
          ), ")"
        )
      )
    )
  )

ggplot(originality_vs_abundance, aes(x = abundance, y = value)) +
  geom_point(color = guild_colors[["pollinator"]], alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~measure, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Abundance (log scale)", y = "Functional originality")
```



### The models

We fit the model of @Coux-etal-2016 and the same model with unweighted
originality, for both responses:

- **ND ~ weighted originality + abundance** (as in Coux et al.)
- **ND ~ originality + abundance**
- and the same two models for **HS**.

All models are mixed models fitted with `INLA`, with site and species as
random intercepts

- **ND** is modelled as a binomial: the number of plants a pollinator visits,
  out of the plants at its site.
- **HS** is modelled as Gaussian, like the linear mixed models of Coux et al.
  That's a crude choice for a measure bounded by 0 and 1, with every
  single-partner species sitting exactly at 1, but it keeps the comparison
  with their analysis honest.

Abundance is log-transformed. All predictors are standardised, so
coefficients are per standard deviation, on the link scale.

```{r}
term_labels <- c(
  originality_z = "Originality",
  originality_w_z = "Originality",
  log_abundance_z = "Log abundance",
  log_n_plants_z = "Log plant richness"
)
response_labels <- c(
  degree = "Normalised degree (binomial)",
  hs = "Specificity, HS (Gaussian)"
)
model_colors <- c(
  `weighted originality` = "grey45",
  originality = guild_colors[["pollinator"]]
)

plot_coefficients <- function(tbl) {
  tbl |>
    filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
    mutate(
      term = factor(
        term_labels[term],
        levels = rev(unique(term_labels))
      ),
      response = factor(
        response_labels[response],
        levels = response_labels
      ),
      model = factor(model, levels = names(model_colors))
    ) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = mean, y = term, color = model)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
    geom_pointrange(
      aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper),
      position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)
    ) +
    scale_color_manual(values = model_colors) +
    facet_wrap(~response, scales = "free_x") +
    labs(
      x = "Posterior mean and 95% credible interval (per SD)",
      y = NULL, color = NULL
    ) +
    theme(legend.position = "top")
}

plot_coefficients(trait_network_models)
```

### Conclusion

Are functionally original pollinators specialists? In these
data, the honest answer is "yes, it seems so":

1. The weighted originality used by @Coux-etal-2016 is partly a measure of
   abundance. In a model that also includes abundance, it takes some of the
   credit for abundance's effect.
2. With unweighted originality, a trait-only measure, the effect on ND is
   weaker, and about half of it goes away once plant richness is accounted
   for.
3. Neither version predicts HS.
